power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Objectives: Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) offers alternative options to patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) unable to tolerate first line treatment.

Randomized controlled trial data suggest efficacy of NMES treatment in improving OSA outcomes, snoring and sleepiness; however, no study to our knowledge has examined the effects on a range of daytime patient reported outcomes in a large real-world sample.
Methods: This report presents clinical data from 472 patients completing NMES treatment.

Bayesian linear mixed models were used to analyze pre-to-post treatment changes in mood (PHQ8), sleep disturbance (PROMIS-SD-4a), sleep related impairment (PROMIS-SRI-4a), and functioning (FOSQ), whilst controlling for key covariates.
Posterior probabilities were calculated to estimate the probability of a change in symptoms (P(effect > 0)) and probability of exceeding a minimal clinically important difference (P(effect > MCID)).
text.formatted: Posterior probabilities were calculated to estimate the probability of a change in symptoms (P(effect > 0)) and probability of exceeding a minimal clinically important difference (P(effect > MCID)).

text.text: Results: The posterior probabilities of an improvement in scores in sleep disturbance (mean change -6.1, 94% HDI: -3.8 to -8.5) and sleep-related impairment (mean change -10.0, 94% HDI: -5.4 to -14), depression (mean change -3.5, 94% HDI: -1.7 to -5.2), at posttreatment were greatest and varied between 99.8 to 100%.
Probability of change in functioning was low (60.9% chance of improvement).
These effects remained when controlling for age, gender, treatment adherence, mean intensity and variance in intensity.
Probabilities for MCI change for mood, sleep disturbance and sleep-related impairment were high (86-91%).
Conclusions: The results from this report highlight the potential impact NMES therapy has on patient reported outcomes.
These findings are in support of prior randomized placebo-controlled data and several observational cohort studies for NMES as treatment for mild OSA.
Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a sleep-related breathing disorder, characterized by repeated reduction (hypopnea) or cessation (apnoea) in airflow during sleep.

Associated sleep disruption and persistent hypoxia may lead to negative health sequelae (Xie et al., 2017) increased risks of accidents (Garbarino et al., 2016; Luzzi et al., 2022), increased risk of Parkinson's disease (Sun et al., 2020), poorer quality of life (Shirisha et al., 2025) and increased risk of depression (Edwards et al., 2020), which yields a major economic burden (Borsoi et al., 2022).

text.text: While the gold-standard treatment Positive Airway Pressure eliminates most of the breathing events, adherence is suboptimal in many patients (Crew et al., 2021; Oliver et al., 2024; Rotenberg et al., 2016).

text.text: While oral appliances are generally more easily tolerated than PAP therapy, effects on dental or occlusal structures remain a concern.
Novel alternatives to PAP therapy and oral appliances have emerged, with a particular focus on the tongue.

The stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve at night after surgical implantation of a device has recently been reported as non-inferior to PAP therapy (Heiser et al., 2023), and associated with improvements in patient reported outcomes (Braun et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The stimulation of the hypoglossal nerve at night after surgical implantation of a device has recently been reported as non-inferior to PAP therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Heiser et al., 2023)</ref>, and associated with improvements in patient reported outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Braun et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, this treatment is indicated only for individuals with moderate to severe OSA and an AHI between 15 and 100/hr, and a BMI ≤ 40kg/m2, intolerant to PAP therapy and without concentric pattern of collapse of the upper airway as determined by sleep endoscopy (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2023).
The latter is an expensive procedure, and the list of indicators means there are limited alternative treatment options for certain OSA patients (e.g., with an AHI <15/h).

text.text: In 1999, a novel, non-implantable therapy based on neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) of the tongue's motor nerves was developed as an alternative to positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment for patients with obstructive sleep apnea (Wiltfang et al., 1999).
text.formatted: In 1999, a novel, non-implantable therapy based on neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) of the tongue's motor nerves was developed as an alternative to positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment for patients with obstructive sleep apnea <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Wiltfang et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: This approach primarily targets the genioglossus muscle, aiming to reduce the likelihood of upper airway collapse during sleep.
A commercial device utilizing this mechanism, the eXciteOSA® (Signifier Medical Technologies) received FDA approval in 2021.

A number of uncontrolled (Baptista et al., 2021; Kotecha et al., 2021; Wessolleck et al., 2018) and one randomized placebo-controlled trial (Abreu et al., 2023) provide support for this alternative treatment option for patients with mild to moderate OSA, in terms of improving snoring, sleepiness, sleep quality and AHI severity.

text.text: The present study aims to add to this emerging literature by examining the impact of treatment on sleep health and functional outcomes in real-world patients given the long-standing evidence of impairment (Garbarino et al., 2020; Walia et al., 2017) with OSA established as an independent risk factor (Kim et al., 2019).

text.text: Specifically, the following questions were addressed: Q1: is there a pre-to-post change in patient reported outcomes (PROs).
Q2: Is there a dose-response relationship between the treatment variables (adherence, intensity and intensity variance) and outcome (patient reported outcomes).

We hypothesized an improvement in sleep disturbance, a reduction in sleep-related impairment and an improvement in depressive symptoms, after treatment with the device, and a dose-response relationship to be present between treatment variables and patient outcomes.
The study design is a retrospective observational study using real-time data collected through the eXciteOSA® app.

Data were recorded prospectively by users during routine use of the app and were accessed for this analysis under an ethics approval by the Department of Psychological Sciences and Health ethics committee (79.19.07.2023.
Data on patient reported outcomes, attention/vigilance, treatment related factors and demographics were extracted.
Participants who provided at baseline and at least one post-treatment questionnaire were selected.
Any follow-up data provided between 30 th of Jan 2022 and the 30th of April 2024 were included in the dataset, data extraction occurred on the 1 st of May 2025.
No other inclusion criteria were set at the data extraction stage.
At the time of data extraction, there were 14,443 eXciteOSA® users.
Individuals who did not complete the 42 sessions or did not have either a baseline and post-treatment questionnaire were excluded from the analysis (n=12,948).
There was a wide range in the duration between the date of post-treatment questionnaire completion and finishing the 42 sessions.

Consequently, and to gather a "valid" post-treatment assessment of PROs, we included in the analysis only those individuals who completed a post-treatment questionnaire within 1 month of finishing their 42 sessions.
This approach left us with a final sample of 469 individuals, see Figure 1 for details.

The Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire 10 is the short version of the full scale.

Through ten items it assesses impact of sleepiness on daytime functioning (Chasens et al., 2009; Weaver et al., 1997), such as "Do you have difficulty concentrating on the things you do because you are sleepy or tired?". scores range from 1 (extreme difficulty) to 4 (no difficulty) with higher scores indicating less impairment.

The Patient Health Questionnaire 8 item version (PHQ-8) assesses mood without the suicidal thoughts question included in the full scale (Kroenke et al., 2001; Kroenke et al., 2009).

and items are rated on a scale from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), higher scores thus indicating worse mood.

Two Patient Reported Outcome Measures Information System (PROMIS) measures were used: Sleep Disturbance to assess sleep disturbances ("In the past 7 days, I had a problem with my sleep") and PROMIS-Sleep Related Impairment to assess daytime impact of sleep problems (e.g., "In the past 7 days, I had a hard time getting things done because I was sleepy").
The 4-item version of each scale was used and items included and scores ranged from 1 to 5 with higher scores indicating worse performance.
Raw scores were converted into a T-score following the PROMIS scoring manual and conversion tables, there were no missing items (PROMIS Health Organization, 2023).

Finally, the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire (Reilly et al., 1993) was included to assess impairment in work productivity and activity with items such as "During the past seven days, how many hours did you miss from work because of your health problems?", scoring followed guidelines (Reilly Associates, n.d.), of the subscales only overall work productivity is reported in the results.

The data were extracted by Signifier Medical Technologies, and the encrypted and passwordprotected file was shared with the two investigators involved in the analysis (AJ and MC) safely through Strathclyde One Drive.

The device (eXciteOSA®, Signifier Medical Technologies) delivers intraoral stimulation for 20 minutes daily over an initial 6-week period, followed by twice-weekly sessions to sustain therapeutic benefits.
The electrical stimulation is applied during the day to enhance tongue muscle tone and endurance, with residual effects that help maintain airway patency at night.
The patient starts each 20-minute session by controlling the device through an app.
Before the first session (and up to the start of the third session), the patient is asked to complete a brief survey about their sleep, mood and daytime functioning.

text.text: To answer the two research questions (is there a pre-to-post change in patient reported outcomes (PROs) and is there a dose-response relationship between the treatment variables (adherence, intensity and intensity variance) and outcome (patient reported outcomes), a Bayesian linear mixed model was applied.

The models included treatment adherence, treatment intensity and intensity variance, age and gender as co-variates, and tested the interaction between pre-and-post timepoints and each PRO questionnaire.

As our model is Bayesian, we were able to compute the posterior probability of effects being in a given direction, rather than the probability of an effect if there were no difference, as in null hypothesis significance testing.
For example, we can compute the probability that post-treatment scores are on average greater than pretreatment scores for our PRO variables.
We also explored how many individuals report symptoms below clinically relevant cut-offs at post-treatment.
To answer this question, we applied posteriorpredictive simulation, a Bayesian statistical approach that generates many new datasets from a fitted model.

These datasets represent distributions of individuals, rather than means, and allow for the estimation of the probability that an individual starting above a particular cut-off would fall below it after treatment.

For the two PROMIS scales (sleep-related impairment and sleep disturbance), the cut-off score was 55, for the PHQ-8 a cut off of ≥ 10 was considered for current depression (Kroenke et al., 2009) and for the FOSQ-10, a cut off of 17.9 was considered, with lower scores indicating worse functioning (Weaver et al., 2007).

The study results should be interpreted in light of both strengths and limitations.
The sample size and real-world data were strengths.
The sample size was larger than any previous study published evaluating this device.

The real-world nature captures data from individuals who are not selectively agreeing to participate in clinical trials, which usually includes more educated, female, and less symptomatic individuals who have also been evaluated against stringent inclusion/exclusion criteria.
Thus, this real-world sample represents a broader clinical and perhaps more generalizable population.
Lastly, validated questionnaires were used, including those where standardized scores are available to compare to normative values (e.g., PROMIS).
The limitations of this study included sample selection and lack of control group.
We were only able to analyze data from individuals who had completed at least two questionnaires on the app.
While the baseline question was compulsory, this requirement was not the case for the VA users (approx. 20% of all users).
The need to complete questionnaires was removed for all users referred through the VA system in the USA.
We also did not have data on OSA severity or which of the participants had mild OSA vs primary snoring, which could have been an important covariate.
Without a placebo control group, we were unable to rule out effects such as regression to the mean or expectation of change.
To estimate the contribution of regression to the mean (RTM) to the observed improvement in depressive symptoms, we adapted Linden's (2013) equations 5 and 6.

In Linden's approach, the distance between a subgroup's baseline mean and the population mean (Cσ) is estimated from the cut-off used to select that subgroup; as participants in the present study were not selected on PHQ-8 score, this distance could instead be calculated directly from the observed baseline mean (x̄ -μ).

Substituting this value into Linden's equation 6 gives an expected post-test mean in the absence of treatment of μ + ρ(x̄ -μ), with the expected RTM effect being the difference between this value and the observed baseline mean.

We used a reference mean (μ) of 6.6, the baseline mean of a large sample of adults with chronic conditions (Ory et al., 2013), and an 11-day test-retest reliability (ρ) of .83 for the PHQ-8 total score (Mattsson et al., 2020).

text.text: Despite these limitations, this report provides evidence for the impact of a neuromuscular electrical stimulation on patient-reported outcomes.
The findings demonstrate that NMES therapy is associated with clinically relevant improvements in multiple patient-reported outcomes in a large real-world cohort.
These results add to the evidence base established by prior randomised and observational studies supporting NMES as a therapeutic option for individuals with mild OSA or primary snoring.
The results need to be supplemented with future placebo-controlled trials using both subjective and objective measures of functioning.
